subject: is anything different between this bugs/jags and stan model?

messages.author: e591fcf77457775e
messages.subject: is anything different between this bugs/jags and stan model?
parts:
hi and thanks in advance for any assistance.

I've migrated a model from MLwiN to first BUGS and then JAGS and now STAN in hopes of overcoming memory limitations and secondarily speeding estimation times.
I get essentially similar estimated parameters from MLwiN, BUGS and JAGS. Stan runs fine - although not faster as hoped for - but one variance estimation (term sigma2.u3 below) is off by several orders of magnitude. I wonder if i erred in porting my model code. 

any optimization/reparameterization suggestions are welcome, but my first goal is getting results that make sense.

Here is BUGS/JAGS code:

model
{
 # Level 1 definition
 for(i in 1:N) {
      alpha[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i],tau)


       mu[i]<- beta[1] + beta[2] * v_pred[i] + u2[group[i]]  + u3[id[i],1]  + u3[id[i],2] * pred[i]
 }


 # Higher level definitions
 for (j in 1:n2) {
    u2[j] ~ dnorm(0,tau.u2)
 }
 for (j in 1:n3) {
    u3[j,1:2] ~ dmnorm(zero3[1:2], tau.u3[1:2,1:2])
 }


 # Priors for fixed effects
 for (k in 1:18) { beta[k] ~ dflat() }


 # Priors for random terms
 tau ~ dgamma(0.001000,0.001000)
 sigma2 <- 1/tau
 tau.u2 ~ dgamma(0.001000,0.001000)
 sigma2.u2 <- 1/tau.u2


 for (i in 1:2) { zero3[i] <- 0 }


 tau.u3[1:2,1:2] ~ dwish(R3[1:2, 1:2],2)
 sigma2.u3[1:2,1:2] <- inverse(tau.u3[,])
}
 


here is the STAN code:

data {
    int<lower=1> N; //  number of rows
    int<lower=1> n2; // number of groups
    int<lower=1> n3; // number of individuals
    int<lower=0,upper=1> pred[N];
    int<lower=1, upper=n2> group[N];
    int<lower=1, upper=n3> id[N];
    real alpha[N]; 

    cov_matrix[2] R3;  // R3 = matrix(c(0.002,0,0,0.002), nrow=2)

    int<lower=0,upper=1>    v_pred[N];
}

transformed data {
  vector[2] gamma_mu;    

  cov_matrix[2] invR;
  invR <- inverse(R3);

  gamma_mu[1] <- 0;
  gamma_mu[2] <- 0;
}

parameters {
 real<lower=-5, upper=5> beta[2];   // Priors for fixed effects (uniform)
 real u2[n2];
 vector[2] u3[n3];


 real<lower=0> sigmasq_u2; // Date-level vol
 real<lower=0> sigmasq_alpha; // Data-level vol


 cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
 
}


transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma_u2;       // sigma in original bugs model
  real<lower=0> sigma_alpha;
  sigma_u2 <- sqrt(sigmasq_u2);
  sigma_alpha <- sqrt(sigmasq_alpha);
}

model {
      real alpha_mu[N];

      for(p in 1:N) {
         alpha_mu[p] <- beta[1]
         + beta[2] * v_pred[p]
         + u2[group[p]]
         + u3[id[p], 1]
         + u3[id[p], 2] * pred[p];
      }

      // # Priors for random coefficients:
      sigmasq_u2 ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
      sigmasq_alpha ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);

      u2 ~ normal(0, sigma_u2);

      // Priors for random terms
      alpha ~ normal(alpha_mu, sigma_alpha);

      for (j in 1:n3) u3[j] ~ multi_normal(gamma_mu, Sigma);
      // # Hyper-priors:
      Sigma ~ inv_wishart(2, invR);
}


thx, J

You should take a look at Andrew's paper on priors for
variance. We don't recommend these priors. Conjugacy
carries no advantages in Stan's computations, either.

> u2 ~ normal(0, sigma_u2);
>
> // Priors for random terms

You could apply the Matt trick here.

>

> // # Hyper-priors:
> Sigma ~ inv_wishart(2, invR);

You might want to check out our lkj priors.

Eventually, we'll have support to do all this directly
with Cholesky factors for Sigma, which should be much more
efficient.

- Bob

Also, are you using the same initial values? By default, Stan starts

BUGS samples from the posterior.

Also, are you measuring effective samples per second, or just iteration

estimators to compare apples to apples, but R2WinBUGS and R2jags and RStan

whereas RStan uses the within-across chain estimators described in our doc
and in the 3rd edition of Bayesian Data Analysis).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] is anything different between this bugs/jags and stan model?
parts:
We've been exploring the Matt trick more, and its efficacy
depends on the amount of data. The less data there is, the
more effective it is.

The LKJ priors let you do things like shrink to the unit
correlation matrix and put independent priors on scale. It's
a more natural prior than Wishart. It's just as efficient in
Stan because we don't do anything special for conjugate priors.
Check out this paper by Ben Goodrich (who's done most of the
multivariate implementations in Stan).

We still haven't fully optimized our multivariate priors, so
they'll get substantially faster in the coming year (I'm guessing
an order of magnitude faster or more).

If the data's big, the time spent computing the likelihood will
dwarf the time spent computing the prior, so it doesn't really matter
what you use for efficiency. Cholesky factoring in the model outside
of the likelihood loop can be a huge time saver. That is, instead of

for (n in 1:N)
y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);

use something lik:

{
matrix[rows(Sigma),rows(Sigma)] L;
L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
for (n in 1:N)
y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu,L);
}

The brackets provide the scope for the local variable L.

- Bob

>
> with very diffuse priors, whereas JAGS takes the mean and I believe

> Also, are you measuring effective samples per second, or just iteration
> speed? Only the former matters for inference and parameter estimation.
> It's a bit tricky, because you need to use the same effective sample size
> estimators to compare apples to apples, but R2WinBUGS and R2jags and RStan
> use different estimators (I believe the former use something from Coda,
> whereas RStan uses the within-across chain estimators described in our doc

>
> Next, there's time to converge, and then mixing speed after convergence.
> HMC (as in Stan) tends to converge in fewer iterations from bad starting points than
> Gibbs (as in BUGS/JAGS).

> setting reasonable inits made a big difference.
